We found that self-explanation prompts are a potentially powerful intervention across a range of instructional conditions.

sources.design: computer-based learning environment for student teachers, solved example problems
sources.effect: instructional explanations reduced self-explanation activity and outcomes vs prompts alone
sources.finding_quote: self-explanation prompts had favorable effects on learning outcomes, whereas instructional explanations can reduce the student teacher's self-explanation activities and thereby the learning outcomes (quoted per ERIC abstract record EJ729810; publisher's own abstract text was paywalled/blocked this session)

backfire.condition: Adding instructional (given) explanations alongside self-explanation prompts crowds out the learner's own self-explanation activity and reduces the outcome self-explanation alone would produce.
Classroom and delayed-retention evidence for self-explanation is much thinner than immediate-post-test evidence.

sources.design: utility-rating review of 10 learning techniques

sources.finding_quote: we discuss 10 learning techniques in detail and offer recommendations about their relative utility... The techniques include elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, summarization, highlighting (or underlining), the keyword mnemonic, imagery use for text learning, rereading, practice testing, distributed practice, and interleaved practice.

backfire.condition: Effect depends on the nature of the question and whether the learner has relevant prior knowledge to orient to; weak or absent on unfamiliar material with no relevant background.

sources.design: 12 studies: rate understanding -> explain mechanism -> re-rate, on devices, phenomena, procedures, narratives
sources.effect: large self-rating drop after explanation attempt; strongest for explanatory knowledge
sources.finding_quote: People feel they understand complex phenomena with far greater precision, coherence, and depth than they really do; they are subject to an illusion—an illusion of explanatory depth. The illusion is far stronger for explanatory knowledge than many other kinds of knowledge, such as that for facts, procedures or narratives. The illusion for explanatory knowledge is most robust where the environment supports real-time explanations with visible mechanisms.

sources.design: 6 studies, construal-level manipulation
sources.effect: IOED reduced by concrete construal
sources.finding_quote: Gap-fill (2026-09-25): now verbatim, fetched directly via the Semantic Scholar API's full abstract field. 'An illusion of explanatory depth (IOED) occurs when people believe they understand a concept more deeply than they actually do. To date, IOEDs have been identified only in mechanical and natural domains... Six studies illustrated that IOEDs occur because people adopt an inappropriately abstract construal style when they assess how well they understand concrete concepts. As this mechanism predicts, participants who naturally adopted concrete construal styles (Study 1) or were induced to adopt a concrete construal style (Studies 2-4 and 6), experienced diminished IOEDs. Two additional studies documented a novel IOED in the social psychological domain of electoral voting (Studies 5 and 6), demonstrating the generality of the construal mechanism.'

sources.design: 3 experiments, political-policy explanations
sources.effect: mechanistic (not reasons-based) explanation reduced IOED and moderated attitudes
sources.finding_quote: Asking people to explain policies in detail both undermined the illusion of explanatory depth and led to attitudes that were more moderate (Experiments 1 and 2). Although these effects occurred when people were asked to generate a mechanistic explanation, they did not occur when people were instead asked to enumerate reasons for their policy preferences.

sources.design: 3 preregistered close/conceptual replications of Fernbach et al. Experiments 2-3
sources.effect: key policy-moderation effects not significant
sources.finding_quote: None of the key effects were statistically significant, and only one survived a small-telescopes analysis. Although participants reported less policy understanding after providing mechanistic policy explanations, policy-position extremity and in-group favoritism were unaffected... providing mechanistic explanations increases people's recognition of their ignorance but is unlikely to increase their political moderation.

replication.result: replicated (core IOED self-rating-drop effect, different materials/theory)

backfire.condition: Effect requires a mechanistic explanation attempt; merely enumerating reasons/opinions does not reduce the illusion.

The downstream claim that reducing IOED also moderates real-world attitudes (political extremism) failed three preregistered replications, even though people did recognize more ignorance after explaining.

sources.cite: Fiorella, L. (2023). Learning by Teaching. In Their Own Words (APA Division 2), 158-166.
sources.design: narrative review chapter by Fiorella (co-author of Fiorella & Mayer 2013/2014) summarising his own and others' learning-by-teaching studies
sources.effect: reviews Fiorella & Mayer 2013/2014, Hoogerheide et al. 2014/2016, Lachner et al. 2018, Kobayashi 2019
sources.finding_quote: Verbatim, fetched from the full-text open PDF, read in full this session. On Fiorella & Mayer 2013/2014: 'college students learned about the Doppler effect with the expectation of teaching or taking a test. Of those expecting to teach, some students actually taught by creating a video lecture intended to teach a fictitious student who does not know about the learning material. On immediate comprehension tests, students who prepared to teach performed similarly, regardless of whether they actually taught on video. However, students who actually taught performed best on a delayed comprehension test.' On modality: 'Hoogerheide and colleagues (2016) found that orally teaching syllogistic reasoning problems on video was more effective than restudying the learning material, but teaching via written explanations was not more effective than restudying. There was not a significant difference in performance between the oral and written explanation groups, so this study could not draw strong conclusions about the role of explanation modality. Lachner and colleagues (2018) took a closer look at differences in the quality of students written and oral explanations and their relationship with different learning outcomes. Written explanations tended to be more organized and contributed to better conceptual understanding; in contrast, oral explanations tended to be more elaborative and contributed to better transfer test performance.'

sources.design: 2 experiments; college students learn the Doppler effect with expectation of teaching (video lecture to a fictitious student) vs taking a test; some who expected to teach actually taught
sources.effect: on immediate tests, preparing-to-teach performed similarly whether or not students actually taught; on a delayed test, actually teaching performed best
sources.finding_quote: Design/finding now corroborated via the Fiorella 2023 review (verbatim, fetched, see above), not via the original abstract, which remains unretrieved this session (ScienceDirect 403; Semantic Scholar/Crossref carry no abstract field).

sources.design: meta-analysis, 28 studies
sources.effect: preparing-to-teach g=0.35; teaching-with-preparation g=0.56
sources.finding_quote: The synthesis of 28 studies indicated that the estimated effect sizes (Hedges' gs) were 0.35 for preparing-to-teach and 0.56 for teaching with preparing-to-teach. Both preparing-to-teach and teaching with preparing-to-teach were effective in promoting deep learning (as well as surface learning) and even after a delay. The learning benefits of teaching with preparing-to-teach were larger when students expected and engaged in an interactive teaching activity than when they expected and engaged in a non-interactive teaching activity.

sources.design: students creating video-based modeling examples (explaining to an audience) vs studying
sources.effect: supports learning-by-explaining benefit
sources.finding_quote: Corroborated indirectly via the Fiorella 2023 review (fetched, above): 'Hoogerheide and colleagues (2014) reported a similar pattern of results in which actually teaching on video led to better understanding than only preparing to teach.' Direct abstract still not retrievable this session (Elsevier paywall; no OA abstract surfaced).

backfire.cite: Hoogerheide, Deijkers, Loyens, Heijltjes & van Gog (2016)
backfire.condition: Gap-fill correction (2026-09-25): the study's own comparison of oral vs written explanation groups was NOT statistically significant, so it 'could not draw strong conclusions about the role of explanation modality' (per the Fiorella 2023 review, fetched directly). The title's framing ('not from writing to them') overstates the data. Direct abstract text still not retrievable this session.

Gap-fill correction (2026-09-25), now directly fetched via ERIC: this is a bidirectional trade-off, not a simple written deficit. N=48 students explained a combustion-engine hypertext orally or in writing. Written explanations were MORE effective for organizing content and conceptual knowledge; oral explanations were MORE effective for transfer, via more elaborative processing. For feynman (a written page), this is reassuring for conceptual knowledge and a caution only for transfer specifically.

sources.design: meta-analysis, 53 studies / 166 comparisons, PS-I vs I-PS
sources.effect: g=0.36 raw [0.20,0.51]; g up to 0.58 high-fidelity PF; bias-corrected g=0.87
sources.finding_quote: Our results showed a significant, moderate effect in favor of PS-I (Hedge's g 0.36 [95% confidence interval 0.20; 0.51]). The effects were even stronger (Hedge's g ranging between 0.37 and 0.58) when PS-I was implemented with high fidelity to the principles of Productive Failure (PF)... Contrasting trends were, however, observed for younger age learners (second to fifth graders) and for the learning of domain-general skills, for which effect sizes favored I-PS. Overall, an estimation of true effect sizes after accounting for publication bias suggested a strong effect size favoring PS-I (Hedge's g 0.87).

sources.design: systematic review + meta-analysis, 29 reports / 33 experiments, random-assignment studies 2008-2018
sources.n: k=33 performance; k=14 time; k=11 calibration; n=2799 performance
sources.effect: performance g=-0.25; expository g=-0.32; narrative g=-0.04 (n.s.); time g=0.08 (n.s.); calibration g=0.20 (paper better)
sources.finding_quote: Based on random effects models, reading from screens had a negative effect on reading performance relative to paper (g = -.25). Based on moderator analyses, this may have been limited to expository texts (g = -.32) as there was no difference with narrative texts (g = -.04)... No reliable differences were found for reading time (g = .08). Readers had better calibrated (more accurate) judgement of their performance from paper compared to screens (g = .20). Readers may be more efficient and aware of their performance when reading from paper compared to screens.

sources.design: integrative review of complacency and automation-bias literatures
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: Automation complacency occurs under conditions of multiple-task load, when manual tasks compete with the automated task for the operator's attention. Automation complacency is found in both naive and expert participants and cannot be overcome with simple practice. Automation bias results in making both omission and commission errors when decision aids are imperfect. Automation bias occurs in both naive and expert participants, cannot be prevented by training or instructions, and can affect decision making in individuals as well as in teams.

sources.design: systematic review, decision-support-system literature
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: title/authorship/year confirmed via Crossref (JAMIA, 19(1), 121-127); no abstract field returned this session, so no verbatim quote obtained

sources.design: systematic review, 40/890 studies meeting inclusion criteria
sources.effect: automation bias found in single-task settings tied to verification complexity, not only multitasking
sources.finding_quote: Contrary to the prevailing human factors view, AB was found in single tasks, typically involving diagnosis rather than monitoring, and with high verification complexity... AB appears to be associated with the degree of cognitive load experienced in decision tasks, and appears to not be uniquely associated with multitasking. Strategies to minimize AB might focus on cognitive load reduction.

sources.design: N=199, 3 cognitive-forcing UI designs vs 2 explainable-AI baselines vs no-AI baseline
sources.effect: cognitive forcing reduced overreliance but was rated less favorably; benefited high-Need-for-Cognition users more
sources.finding_quote: People supported by AI-powered decision support tools frequently overrely on the AI: they accept an AI's suggestion even when that suggestion is wrong. Adding explanations to the AI decisions does not appear to reduce the overreliance and some studies suggest that it might even increase it... The results demonstrate that cognitive forcing significantly reduced overreliance compared to the simple explainable AI approaches. However, there was a trade-off: people assigned the least favorable subjective ratings to the designs that reduced the overreliance the most.

replication.cite: Goddard, Roudsari & Wyatt (2012) and Lyell & Coiera (2016)
replication.result: replicated (two independent systematic reviews both find automation bias a robust, frequent phenomenon; Lyell & Coiera refine rather than fail to replicate the conditions)

backfire.condition: Cognitive-forcing interventions that reduce overreliance most are liked least, and their benefit is concentrated in users already disposed to effortful thinking -- risk of abandonment or rubber-stamping by other users.
